scenes.title: Where and when
narration: American dancer and choreographer Steve Paxton originates Contact Improvisation in 1972.

During a tour with the Grand Union collective at Oberlin College in January 1972, Paxton teaches morning somatic sessions called the Small Dance alongside athletic afternoon rehearsals that explore disorientation, falls, rolls, and collisions.
This work produces Magnesium, a seminal performance on gym mats where young male students throw their bodies into unbalance.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Emerging in the counter-cultural aftermath of the late 1960s, contact improvisation is conceived as an egalitarian, anti-spectacular practice that echoes Yvonne Rainer's No Manifesto.
Rejecting choreographic hierarchy, theatrical illusion, and gendered partnering roles, the form frames dance as real-time physical research and mutual listening.
Practitioners dance globally in weekly community jams, multi-day residential festivals like the Breitenbush Jam and Earthdance gatherings, educational conservatories, and performance art venues.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: An ongoing physical dialogue between two or more movers unfolds, governed by gravity, momentum, friction, and shared weight.
Rather than counting beats or executing fixed choreographic phrases, dancers maintain continuous physical contact, listening kinesthetically through a rolling point of touch.
Watch for the Small Dance, the Aikido Roll, and the Table-Top.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Sources do not describe a specific musical tradition, meter, or prescribed musical accompaniment for Contact Improvisation.
Early performances like Contact Improvisations at the John Weber Gallery take place alongside ambient gallery elements and a concurrent film screening of George Manupelli's Dr. Chicago.

Contact Improvisation has no set instrumentation, score, or tempo described in primary sources, while jams and stagings unfold in complete acoustic silence punctuated only by audible breath, feet sliding on wood, clothes brushing against canvas or skin, and the dull thuds of body weight dropping onto sprung floors or mats.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Participants dance casually in comfortable, non-restrictive clothing such as sweatpants, tracksuits, leotards, or loose T-shirts chosen specifically to facilitate movement and friction while avoiding zippers or hard hardware.
Contact improvisation takes place in open studios, residential dance centers, art galleries, bookstores, and theaters, usually on sprung wooden floors, gym mats, or tatami.
The physical environment is informal and non-hierarchical, designed for uninhibited rolling and floor work.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key originators and organizers include founder Steve Paxton, along with Nancy Stark Smith, who dances in the earliest performances, establishes the Contact Newsletter, co-edits Contact Quarterly, and develops the Underscore; Lisa Nelson, pioneer of Tuning Scores and video documentation; early Oberlin and Bennington collaborators Nita Little and Curt Siddall; Daniel Lepkoff; Mary Fulkerson; Barbara Dilley; and Nancy Topf.
Following its Manhattan debut, the practice disperses through regional North American centers including New York, Boston, San Francisco, and Montreal.
The form develops out of 1960s postmodern dance, the Judson Dance Theater, and the Grand Union collective.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Steve Paxton draws directly upon aikido falling and rolling techniques to ensure safety during momentum-driven collisions.
Paxton develops the form following his professional training in the companies of Merce Cunningham and José Limón.
The practice remains rooted in the 1960s experimental collective where Paxton, Barbara Dilley, and Yvonne Rainer question the conventions of dance.

scenes.title: Try one step
narration: Stand upright in stillness with eyes open or soft, noticing micro-weight shifts and postural adjustments along the vertical axis during the Small Dance.
Soften your knees, curve your spine diagonally, and roll smoothly across the floor along the diagonal of the back without striking bony prominences in the Aikido Roll.
Count 1-2-3-4 then 5-6-7-8 across eight counts and two bars.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 explores first steps, focusing today on cultivating internal postural awareness and smooth floor rolling.
This is Level 1: Sensing Gravity, with an intermediate overall difficulty.
An experienced somatic practitioner instructs with quiet precision, focusing on physical sensations, anatomy, and balance rather than theatrical presentation.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Keep your body relaxed, alert, and grounded with softened joints, ready to yield to gravity or absorb a partner's weight.
Use limbs primarily as responsive sensors and structural supports rather than decorative gestures, minimizing grasping in favor of continuous rolling contact.
The ribcage, pelvis, and back serve as primary fulcrums for weight exchange, rolling to share and redirect gravitational mass.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1 is the Small Dance: stand upright in stillness with eyes open or soft, noticing micro-weight shifts and postural adjustments along the vertical axis.
Step 2 is the Aikido Roll: soften your knees, curve your spine diagonally, and roll smoothly across the floor across the diagonal of the back without striking bony prominences.
Footwork remains uncodified, shifting fluidly between barefoot floor contact, weight-bearing lunges, and suspended flight.
Drill this by standing in the Small Dance for 3 minutes, tracking micro-sways in the feet.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); three repetitions of every step before moving on
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3 is Table-Top Support: drop to hands and knees with a stable spine, allowing a partner to drape or roll their torso across your back.
Step 4 is the Rolling Point of Contact: make physical touch with a partner's arm, back, or shoulder, moving together without sliding while rolling the contact point continuously across surfaces.
Drill this by practicing aikido shoulder rolls along diagonal lines across the mat.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Rest back-to-back with a partner, finding mutual equilibrium without moving feet.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full
